prompt: A boat sails $5$ km, turns so the angle inside the triangle at the turn is $120^\circ$, then sails $16$ km. A friend takes the straight route from the start point to the finish point. How many kilometers shorter is the straight route than the boat's path?
hint: This is two steps: first find the straight-line distance, then compare it with the sailed distance.

hints.text: This is two steps: first find the straight-line distance, then compare it with the sailed distance.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Legs of $3$ km and $5$ km with a $120^\circ$ turn: $c^2 = 9 + 25 + 15 = 49$, so straight $= 7$ km while the path is $3 + 5 = 8$ km. The saving is $8 - 7 = 1$ km. Now do the same two steps with $5$ and $16$.

explanation: Step 1 — the straight route uses the Law of Cosines: $c^2 = 5^2 + 16^2 - 2(5)(16)\cos 120^\circ$.
Step 2 — the boat actually sailed $5 + 16 = 21$ km.
The straight route is $21 - 19 = 2$ km shorter.

alternativeExplanations.title: Two numbers on a number line
steps: Mark the sailed distance, 21 km, on a number line.
Mark the straight distance, 19 km, just to its left.
The gap between the marks IS the saving: 2 km. Drawing both numbers keeps you from answering with 19 by mistake.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the saving is so small
steps: A 120° turn is a gentle bend — the boat almost keeps going straight.
A nearly straight path is barely longer than the true straight line, so the shortcut saves very little.
If the turn had been 90°, the straight line would be about 16.8 km and the saving would jump to about 4.2 km.
